newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn draws fire as budget freeze not ruled out.
newsitem.headline: Bonn draws fire as budget freeze not ruled out.

text.p: Trade unions and opposition politicians on Sunday attacked the German finance ministry's failure to rule out the possibility of an imminent spending freeze, saying such a move would hit jobs harder in a time of high unemployment.
A freeze would be seen to be helping the federal government in its efforts to reduce public deficits ahead of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Speculation about a freeze has increased recently following the higher-than-expected increase in January unemployment, which in turn is seen leading to a higher burden on state finances.

But the German Federation of Trade Unions (DGB) said any spending freeze would in fact dent job creation even more because it would probably be centred around public investment in areas from construction projects to research.
"Such a measure would have significant disadvantages for growth and employment," DGB board member Michael Geuenich said on Sunday.
A ministry spokesman said in response to enquiries on Saturday that German Finance Minister Theo Waigel was not ruling out the possibility of a budget freeze in the next few weeks.
But asked to comment on a magazine report that Waigel planned to take the step in the coming week, he added that a final decision had not been made.
If the freeze goes ahead, additional spending over a certain amount would have to personally authorised by Waigel. Such a measure would be designed to save billions of marks of state spending.

The parliamentary budget spokesman for the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), Karl Diller, forecast an additional budgetary deficit this year of some 10 billion marks partly as a result of rising jobless levels, but said a budget freeze was not the answer.
He said that such freezes meant that planned-for state investments did not ultimately go ahead, thus destroying business confidence in the economy and the creation of jobs.
